lines: A source quietly starts feeding duplicate rows into a revenue table, and nobody notices for days.
By the time someone does notice, the team's very first move isn't fixing anything.
It's trying to figure out which of the many dashboards downstream of that table are actually affected.
And nobody in the room had ever actually run that query before that night.
Here's the loop this whole topic walks through, start to finish, on that exact incident.
Detect that something's wrong, then triage how severe and how wide it actually is.
Contain it so it stops spreading, then repair only what's actually broken.
And finally, write a postmortem -- not to assign blame, but to make the same failure harder to repeat.
Worth pausing on this before it's answered.
Dozens of dashboards sit somewhere downstream of the table that just went bad.
Is the safe move simply notifying every single one of them, just in case?
Or is there a better way to know exactly who's actually affected?
steps.answer: No, notifying everyone isn't the safe default -- it trains people to ignore the next real alert. The better answer is computing exactly which downstream pieces genuinely depend on the broken one.

lines: Here's how that computation actually works.
A pipeline's own asset graph already declares which things depend on which other things.
Walking those declared connections tells you, with certainty, exactly which downstream pieces are genuinely at risk.
Nobody has to remember the dependency map, because the map was never hand-kept to begin with.
steps.takeaway: A guessed blast radius either misses someone or wakes everyone. A computed one does neither.

lines: One more question worth asking before the answer's shown.
A handful of the table's own partitions hold the actual bad rows.
Does containing this incident mean deleting those bad partitions right away?
Or is there a reason to leave them alone, at least for now?
steps.answer: No, don't delete them yet. Mark those partitions as quarantined and stop anything downstream from reading them -- deleting first destroys the exact evidence a later postmortem will need.

lines: Here's that pattern, named directly.
Containing the incident means marking only the affected partitions and halting whatever reads from them -- nothing is erased.
Repairing it later means reloading only those same marked partitions, and nothing else in the table.
Both steps touch exactly the part that's actually wrong, and nothing more.
steps.takeaway: Containment and repair both work the same way: touch exactly the partitions that are actually wrong.

lines: Here's who actually runs all of this, sourced directly from a well-known incident-management account rather than invented for this course.
One person holds the overall state of the incident and decides who does what.
A second person is the only one actually allowed to touch the system while the incident is live.
A third person speaks for the whole team to everyone else, so updates don't come from five different directions at once.
Pulling it together now.
Detect, then triage how bad it really is, then contain by marking rather than deleting, then repair only the marked part.
Finally, a postmortem that assumes good intentions throughout and looks for what the system itself should have caught.
The hook's real cost wasn't the duplicate rows themselves. It was every hour spent simply guessing who else was touched.
steps.takeaway: The hook's real cost wasn't the duplicate rows. It was the hours spent guessing who else was affected.

lines: One real test to close on, run against an actual pipeline's own asset graph rather than just described.
A good number of downstream dashboards genuinely sit somewhere below this shop's own pipeline.
Running the real lineage computation against that real graph, how many of those dashboards does it actually implicate?
Almost all of them, because they all share the same pipeline somewhere upstream -- or a small, exact handful?
steps.answer: Only a small, exact handful. The real graph's own declared connections single out a specific subset as genuinely downstream of the incident, and every other dashboard was never actually at risk at all.
